target.title: fix(ai): record token usage on Responses early-abort (#100954)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Azure/OpenAI Responses streams that end early with `response.incomplete` (e.g. `max_output_tokens` reached, content filter) never send `response.completed`. Both Responses stream processors on `main` assign `output.usage` **only** inside the `response.completed` branch, so these early-terminated streams leave usage — and its cost — at zero, dropping the reported token counts (including partial cache-hit tokens) and their cost from telemetry and session accounting. This is the drift described in #100954.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `response.incomplete` event carries a full `Response` object with the same `usage` shape (`input_tokens` / `output_tokens` / `total_tokens` + `input_tokens_details`) as `response.completed`. The fix records that usage — **and computes its cost** — when the stream terminates early.

Two processors handle Responses streams and both had the identical completed-only defect, so both are fixed:
- `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.ts`
- `src/agents/openai-transport-stream.ts`

In each, the terminal usage+cost logic is extracted into a shared `recordResponsesTerminalUsage` helper (map usage → `calculateCost` → service-tier pricing) that both `response.completed` and the new `response.incomplete` branch call. Cost must run for the incomplete path too because session accounting sums `usage.cost.total` (`src/agents/sessions/agent-session.ts`); recording tokens without cost would still under-report. Stop-reason mapping and completed-only backfill stay specific to `response.completed`. The abort lifecycle already forwards a populated `output.usage` into the emitted error event, so no changes to the abort path or the generic `normalizeUsage` were needed.

## User Impact

Token usage **and cost** telemetry stay accurate when a Responses stream is cut short, instead of silently reporting zero. No change to normal (`response.completed`) streams or to provider defaults.

## Evidence

Reproduction and after-fix behavior are exercised by regression tests that drive a real `response.incomplete` event (carrying nonzero tokens, including cache reads/writes) through the actual stream processors with **no** `response.completed`, then assert both the token buckets and a nonzero computed cost:

- `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.test.ts` → **35 passed** (new early-abort test asserts `usage.cost.total > 0` and exact per-bucket cost)
- `src/agents/openai-transport-stream.test.ts` → **298 passed** (same regression added for the sibling processor)
- `src/agents/usage.normalization.test.ts` → **10 passed**
- Type check (`tsgo` core project) → clean

Note on live proof: a redacted real-Azure early-abort transcript would require forcing `max_output_tokens`/content-filter termination against a live deployment, which I can't capture here. The regression tests instead feed the exact SDK `response.incomplete` event shape (per the OpenAI Node `ResponseIncompleteEvent` → `Response.usage` contract) through the unmodified processors, so they exercise the real terminal code path rather than a mock.

Closes #100954

---
This is AI-assisted work.

target.title: feat(linux): ship deb/AppImage bundles on stable main-based releases
target.body:
Related: #106337

## What Problem This Solves

Linux companion bundles (deb/AppImage, added in #106352/#106533) exist only as CI artifacts; nothing ships them to users. Releases need a wired, repeatable path that attaches installable Linux packages to the GitHub release for a tag.

## Why This Change Was Made

New operator-dispatched `Linux App Release` workflow, mirroring the Windows installer promotion pattern:

- takes an existing release tag, validates the format, and **rejects prerelease (alpha/beta) tags** — their semver suffix maps to a Debian revision that sorts after the plain stable version, breaking beta-to-stable upgrades; numeric stable revisions (`vYYYY.M.PATCH-N`) order correctly and are allowed
- **requires the tag commit to be reachable from `main`** (Linux bundles ship for main-based releases only)
- builds on **ubuntu-22.04** as the glibc floor so bundles run on Ubuntu 22.04/Debian 12 (PR CI build pinned to match)
- **stamps the release version into the bundles** via a Tauri config override (committed manifests keep a placeholder 0.1.0), and verifies the resulting `.deb` Version field before upload
- attaches `OpenClaw-<version>-amd64.{deb,AppImage}` plus `SHA256SUMS.linux-app.txt` to the GitHub release with `gh release upload --clobber`

Docs updated: `docs/platforms/linux.md` documents the release assets, install commands, and the AppImage FUSE 2 prerequisite (`libfuse2`/`libfuse2t64`, or `APPIMAGE_EXTRACT_AND_RUN=1`); `apps/linux/README.md` documents the release workflow and its stable-only gate.

## User Impact

Linux users can install OpenClaw's desktop companion from GitHub release assets instead of building from source. Operators get a one-dispatch workflow per stable release. No runtime or CLI behavior changes.

## Evidence

- `actionlint` clean on both workflows; `docs:map:check` clean.
- The exact build command and bundle output were live-verified in #106533 (deb built, apt-installed, and run end-to-end on Ubuntu 26.04; AppImage launch smoke) and on fresh Wayland (labwc) boxes via Crabbox where the packaged deb app rendered the full Control UI dashboard end-to-end (CLI discovery, gateway bring-up, dashboard --json auth, WebKitGTK rendering) with only cosmetic warnings.
- Autoreview (Codex gpt-5.6-sol, xhigh): clean after five accepted findings were fixed across rounds — version stamping + deb metadata verification, glibc build floor, prerelease-tag rejection, numeric-revision tags allowed, FUSE prerequisite documented.
- Workflow is dispatch-only; nothing runs until a release operator invokes it, so there is no CI-behavior change on PRs beyond the runner pin.

target.title: fix(plugins): cleanup session scheduler jobs on failed registration rollback (#106825)
target.body:
Closes #106825

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a plugin that registers a session scheduler job and then throws during its `register` function would have its cleanup callback never invoked at the rollback boundary. The live session-scheduler record remained in module-global runtime state while the registry metadata was correctly restored — leaving external plugin-owned scheduler work (via `cleanup`) uncancelled after a failed registration.

## Why This Change Was Made

The registration rollback (`createPluginRegistrationTransaction`) restores the registry snapshot and calls `rollbackPluginGlobalSideEffects` to clean up commands, interactive handlers, code-mode namespaces, context engines, and hooks — but did not clean up session scheduler jobs. These jobs are stored in two layers: a `registry.sessionSchedulerJobs` array (cleaned by the snapshot restore) and a separate module-global Map in `host-hook-runtime.ts` (previously never cleaned on rollback).

The fix adds the existing `cleanupPluginSessionSchedulerJobs` call to the `rollbackPluginGlobalSideEffects` function in `registry.ts`, filtered to the rolling-back plugin's records. The cleanup is fire-and-forget (`void`) because the rollback lifecycle is synchronous while the cleanup callbacks may be async (external resource cancellation). Any cleanup failures are logged as warnings via `pushDiagnostic`.

## User Impact

Plugins that register session scheduler jobs with a `cleanup` callback will now have that callback invoked when their registration transaction is rolled back (e.g., a later exception during the same `register` function). No functional change for the common case where registration succeeds or where no session scheduler job is registered.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(commitments): avoid quadratic heartbeat session discovery
target.body:
Related: #105787

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes heartbeat commitment fan-out latency when many due commitments belong to one session. The existing path loads and expires the JSON store while holding the queue/file lock, releases that lock, then scans the returned in-memory records. For every qualifying due record it rescans the complete store to count recent sent commitments. The quadratic scan is outside the lock, but it delays heartbeat processing and increases heartbeat latency. Reported isolated medians were approximately 191 ms at 1,000, 847 ms at 2,000, and 2.28 s at 4,000 records.

## Why This Change Was Made

The commitments store now builds the rolling 24-hour sent-count map once per agent and reuses it for due-session discovery and single-session due selection. Due-window, snooze, expiry, daily-cap, ordering, limit, agent-scope, queue, and cross-process file-lock behavior remain on the existing path.

This is intentionally an interim JSON-store fix. OpenClaw's shared SQLite state schema already contains a commitments table and indexes, but making it canonical requires a separate JSON-to-SQLite migration/doctor contract and broader persistence coverage. That migration remains a follow-up rather than expanding this focused latency fix.

## User Impact

Heartbeat commitment discovery changes from repeated full-store counting to one aggregation pass plus the existing due-record scan. Large concentrated sessions therefore scale linearly with store size instead of quadratically, without changing which sessions are eligible for delivery.

## Evidence

- Store correctness coverage includes due windows, snoozes, rolling daily caps, agent scope, deterministic session-key ordering, expiry, and concurrent file-store updates.
- The concentrated-session regression uses 8,000 due records in one session and a production-like `limit: 10`, so the base implementation repeatedly rescans the store while the fixed implementation reuses one count map.

target.title: fix(codex): bound app-server websocket handshake waits at 30s
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators using Codex app-server over `websocket`/`unix` transport would hang forever on `initialize`/RPC when a peer accepted TCP but never completed the WebSocket upgrade. Pending frames never flush and the client never sees a transport exit, so the run cannot fail closed or reconnect.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Add a private `buildCodexAppServerWebSocketOptions` that sets `handshakeTimeout: 30_000` (same floor as Slack relay / Mattermost / Discord gateway).
- Both TCP and Unix upgrade paths consume that builder.
- Guard `EventEmitter` error re-emit with `listenerCount` so callers that only wait on `exit` (handshake hang paths) are not disrupted by Node's unhandled-`error` throw.
- Regressions observe production wiring in source (knip-safe) and prove stalled-handshake exit + `initialize` failure with a short test-only hang floor.

No new config/env surface.

## User Impact

**Before:** A Codex app-server endpoint that accepted TCP without completing the websocket handshake could pin `initialize`/RPC forever on that attempt.

**After:** Handshake waits fail closed after 30s (`Opening handshake has timed out` → transport `exit` / client error), so the run can stop or recover instead of hanging.

## Evidence

Head: `a02be68e1107857c4808cc9e93e1af5b10c7f1f1`

### Wiring + hang regression

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```text
[codex handshake negative control] outcome=still-pending readyState=0 wait_ms=300 without_handshakeTimeout=true
[codex handshake proof] timed_out=true elapsed_ms=200 code=1006 handshakeTimeout_ms=200 production_ms=30000
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** TCP-accept / never-upgrade pins Codex app-server `initialize`/RPC with no transport exit.
- **Canonical path:** production `createWebSocketTransport` → private builder with `handshakeTimeout: CODEX_APP_SERVER_WS_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS` (30s).
- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime TCP; real `ws` against loopback `net.Server` that accepts but never upgrades (no handshake mock).
- **Negative control:** plain `ws.WebSocket` **without** `handshakeTimeout` stays `CONNECTING` / `still-pending` after 300ms on the same fixture.
- **After fix:** short test floor exits ~200ms with code 1006; production wiring asserts the 30s constant.
- **CI note:** unrelated `test-extension` readdirSync flake on compact-small-1.

AI-assisted.

target.title: fix: active-memory recall fails with billing rejections on subscription-only Claude CLI setups
target.body:
Closes #106839
Related: #86761

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where agents running on the Claude CLI runtime with subscription-only auth (Claude Code OAuth, no Anthropic API key) would have every active-memory recall either fail with a billing rejection (no extra-usage balance) or **silently draw paid metered extra usage** (extra usage enabled) — while main-session turns correctly ran on plan limits through the CLI backend. Anthropic routing direct anthropic-messages calls on subscription tokens to extra-usage billing is long-standing behavior; the embedded runner's direct-API passthrough (`cli_runtime_passthrough_openclaw`) was never a viable path for these credentials.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds an opt-in `RunEmbeddedAgentParams.cliBackendDispatch: "subscription-auth"`: when the run's provider is `claude-cli` — directly or via a canonical `anthropic/<model>` ref whose configured `agentRuntime` is claude-cli — a backend is registered, and the ordered credential selection resolves to subscription (oauth/token) or nothing rather than an API key, the run executes through `runCliAgent` as a one-shot turn. Active-memory recall opts in. The dispatch preserves the embedded run's contracts:

- **Tool restriction is enforced server-side**: `toolsAllow` maps to the selectable-backend surface, bounds the loopback MCP grant (tools outside it can be neither listed nor called, even under bypass permission modes), and restricted runs get an exclusive loopback-only MCP bundle — user/plugin MCP servers are not merged in.
- **Transcript parity**: the run is mirrored into the caller-owned session file (user turn, live tool call/result records, assistant snapshot — flushed immediately on abort), so `persistTranscripts`, timeout partial-text salvage, and the live terminal-search watcher work identically to embedded runs.
- **Isolation**: fresh CLI process per run, no live-session reuse, session-scoped MCP cleanup (never the process-wide loopback server), CLI session bindings dropped from the result.
- **Scope**: claude-cli only; `google-gemini-cli` and custom backends keep the passthrough — their direct-API contracts were not verified and this PR makes no claims about them. An available API key keeps the existing fast passthrough. The core-side provider set could move to a `CliBackendConfig` capability flag if maintainers prefer that seam.

## User Impact

Subscription-only Claude CLI deployments get working active-memory recall on plan limits, consistent with their main turns — instead of failing every turn or silently consuming paid extra usage. Setups with an Anthropic API key see no behavior change. No config changes required; note that CLI-dispatched recalls measured 13.8–16.9s on a dev laptop, so the plugin's default 15s `timeoutMs` is tight — 30s is comfortable.

target.title: feat(exec): deny-over-allow exec approval denylist (#6615)
target.body:
Fixes #6615. Supersedes #92456 (author inactive since 2026-06-12, no response to review, conflicts with main — full credit to @Hidetsugu55 for the STOP-list concept and dual-host enforcement approach, both kept here).

## Update — re-review 2 (clawsweeper P1 blockers resolved)

The previous review's three P1 blockers were "contract declared but not wired." All three are now wired end-to-end, with focused tests on each exact path plus refreshed real-behavior proof. Also merged latest `origin/main` (resolves the CONFLICTING/behind-main note).

- **[P1] Wire `tools.exec.denylist` into config schema + gateway caller** — `denylist` added to the strict zod `ToolExecBaseShape` (`src/config/zod-schema.agent-runtime.ts`, non-empty-pattern refinement) so `openclaw config validate` accepts it and rejects malformed entries; threaded as `execConfigDenylist` through `agent-tools.ts` → `bash-tools.exec.ts` → `processGatewayAllowlist`, unioned across global + per-agent layers (`resolveEffectiveExecDenylist`). Tests: `config.schema-regressions.test.ts`, `bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts`.
- **[P1] Pass denylist hits into node-host `system.run`** — `invoke-system-run.ts` now evaluates the effective denylist (openclaw.json global + per-agent + `exec-approvals.json` file layer) and passes `denylisted`/`denylistReason` into `evaluateSystemRunPolicy`; the model auto-reviewer is hard-blocked on a hit (human-only), and unanalyzable commands fail closed. Tests: `invoke-system-run.test.ts` (+ node denial reason `denylist-hit`).
- **[P1] Add denylist to exec-approval protocol writes** — `ExecApprovalsDenylistEntrySchema` + `denylist` added to `ExecApprovalsPolicyFields` in `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/exec-approvals.ts` so `exec.approvals.set` / `exec.approvals.node.set` round-trip the field. Tests: `exec-approvals-validators.test.ts`.

Two extra hardening changes made while wiring the above:

- **Real defect fix:** `sanitizeExecApprovalPolicy` (`src/infra/exec-approvals.ts`) was silently dropping the defaults-layer `denylist` on every `saveExecApprovals` write — a routine policy write would disarm an operator's STOP list. Now normalized and preserved.
- **Standalone gate:** the gateway host now has an independent `requiresDenylistApproval || …` short-circuit in `processGatewayAllowlist`, so the deny-over-allow guarantee cannot regress even if `requiresExecApproval`'s denylist handling ever changes.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw's exec approvals support allowlists but no denylist: there is no way to force human approval (or denial) for specific dangerous commands when an agent runs at `security=full` / `ask=off`, or when a broad allowlist/durable trust would otherwise auto-approve them. #6615 asks for a deny-over-allow screening layer so commands like `git push --force` or `rm -rf` patterns always require an explicit human decision, regardless of permissive settings.

## Fix

- `src/infra/exec-approvals-denylist.ts`: entry normalization, strict validation (`collectExecDenylistErrors`), and `resolveEffectiveExecDenylist` (de-duplicated union across layers — deny anywhere = deny).
- **Both config layers**: `openclaw.json` `tools.exec.denylist` (global + per-agent) **and** `~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json` (defaults + `*` + agent), wired through both exec hosts (see Update above).
- **Shared pattern language**: denylist patterns reuse the existing allowlist glob compiler via a new `matchesExecGlob` export — no second matcher to keep in sync (`*` → `[^/]*`, `**` → `.*`, `?` → `[^/]`).
- **Deny wins first**: a hit forces approval ahead of `ask=off`, `security=full`, allowlist hits, and durable allow-always trust, on both the gateway exec host and node-host `system.run` (node denial reason `denylist-hit`). Explicit allow-once approval still clears a hit; `security=deny` still wins overall.
- Conservative fallback: unanalyzable command + configured denylist ⇒ approval required, not fail-open. Basename variants and `bash -c "..."` inner payloads are screened.

## Evidence

**Typecheck (repo's real TS-Go checker):** `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:core:test` both clean on this branch. (Stock `tsc` throws a bogus TS4058 in `src/secrets/config-io.ts` that tsgo does not — pre-existing on `main`.)

**Focused tests — all green on the exact paths flagged:**
- `src/infra/exec-approvals-denylist.test.ts` — 19 (normalize/dedupe, both-layer union, exact/glob/basename/wrapper matches, conservative fallback, precedence).
- `src/node-host/exec-policy.test.ts` — 19 and `src/node-host/invoke-system-run.test.ts` — 36 (node-host `system.run` enforcement, config-layer union, human-only, `denylist-hit`).
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts` — 54 (gateway standalone denylist gate at `security=full`/`ask=off`).
- `packages/gateway-protocol/src/exec-approvals-validators.test.ts` — 8 (protocol/file denylist round-trip).
- `src/config/config.schema-regressions.test.ts` — 39 and `src/config/schema.help.quality.test.ts` — 23 (config schema accept/validate + label/help coverage).

> Note: on a host that symlinks `head` to cargo-coreutils, one unrelated pre-existing test (`processGatewayAllowlist > uses a plan-backed enforced command…`) fails on a `/usr/bin/head` vs `/usr/lib/cargo/bin/coreutils/head` path assertion. It is environmental and independent of this PR (our diff to that test file is additive only).

**Real behavior proof** (real decision code path via `node --import tsx`, no test doubles — `git push --force origin main` allowlisted + durable-trusted at `security=full`/`ask=off`, denylist supplied through the openclaw.json config layer exactly as the wired callers do):

```
## BEFORE (control: no denylist configured)
[gateway-host] command="git push --force origin main" security=full ask=off allowlisted=true durable=true -> AUTO-RUN
[node-host]    command="git push --force origin main" -> ALLOWED

## AFTER (denylist configured via openclaw.json tools.exec.denylist)
denylist = [{"pattern":"git push*--force*","reason":"history rewrite"}]
[gateway-host] -> APPROVAL REQUIRED
[node-host]    -> DENIED (denylist-hit)

## AFTER + explicit allow-once approval
[node-host]    -> ALLOWED (approval cleared the hit)
```

## Scope notes

- Contract is now complete across config schema, gateway protocol write schema, gateway host caller, node-host `system.run`, docs/help (`schema.help.ts` + `schema.labels.ts`), tests, and real proof.
- No drive-by refactors.


## Node-host prompt parity (b0164f0fe8a, 2026-07-09)

Review found that the `host=node` `security=full`/`ask=off` fast path invoked `system.run` directly before prepare/approval registration, so a denylist STOP rule hard-denied server-side (`denylist-hit`) instead of raising the documented human allow-once prompt.

Fixed for prompt parity (recommended option):

- The direct fast path is taken only when the caller-visible effective denylist is **known empty**: the `openclaw.json` config layer is empty AND the node approvals-file denylist (fetched via `exec.approvals.node.get`) is known and empty. Fetch failures fail **closed** into the prepare path.
- On the prepare path, the effective denylist (config layer + node approvals-file layer) is evaluated caller-side; a hit forces a registered human approval request even at full/off, mirroring the gateway host: auto-review is excluded (human-only), and `allow-always` is downgraded to one-shot so no durable trust can be minted from a denylist hit.
- Non-matching commands with a configured denylist still auto-run (via the prepare path); setups with no denylist keep the direct fast path.

Focused tests added in `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-node.test.ts`: config-layer hit registers an approval request (no direct denial), approvals-file hit registers an approval request, non-matching denylist auto-runs, known-empty denylist keeps the fast path, approvals fetch failure fails closed to prepare. `vitest run src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-node.test.ts src/infra/exec-approvals-denylist.test.ts src/node-host/exec-policy.test.ts --pool=forks` => 4 files, 146 tests passed; tsgo typecheck clean.

Honest proof status: production decision-function proof and the focused node-host approval-registration tests are in; a live gateway+node prompt -> allow-once -> runs-exactly-once capture is being prepared on a dedicated QA host and will be appended when complete.

Known residual (intentional, documented here): a denylist configured ONLY in the node machine's own local `openclaw.json` remains invisible to the gateway-side caller and still hard-denies server-side (fail-closed). The two operator surfaces this PR documents (`tools.exec.denylist` config layer and the exec-approvals file) now both get prompt parity on host=node.

Related: #106186

AI-assisted: Codex implemented and validated this release-blocker fix.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Android release operators would see the Google Play upload stop during deterministic screenshot capture when the connected Gateway fixture placed the `Add Gateway` section below the initial composed viewport. The release lane captured four screenshots, then timed out before building or uploading the Play bundle.

## Why This Change Was Made

The gateway scene now waits for the Gateway detail screen's always-visible subtitle instead of a lower-page control. The focused test locks the complete five-scene roster and rejects the viewport-dependent marker. No production UI or fixture behavior changes.

This branch also carries the pending Android 2026.7.2 release metadata from the frozen release candidate so the exact blocked candidate remains reviewable.

## User Impact

Android release automation can finish the connected Gateway screenshot and continue to signed artifact construction and Play upload. App users see no UI change.

- Before: `pnpm android:release:upload` on `f9f65bf019d9` captured home, chat, voice, and settings, then timed out waiting for `Add Gateway`; no Play upload or mobile release ref occurred.

target.title: feat: expose readable session presentation metadata
target.body:
Closes #106793

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where session-list clients must reverse-engineer opaque routing keys such as `agent:main:telegram:main:direct:…` to render a useful session picker. That leaks Gateway-internal naming rules into every client and makes it easy to expose peer or machine identifiers.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds an additive, non-sensitive `presentation` object to each `sessions.list` row. The Gateway now owns session-family classification and projects a client-ready title, optional subtitle, agent/channel/account context, main/background state, and peer kind without exposing peer IDs, transcript text, or filesystem paths.

The raw session key remains the routing identity. Existing clients can ignore the new object, and newer clients can use it without parsing opaque key tails.

## User Impact

Session clients can show readable labels such as “Main session,” “Telegram direct message,” “Scheduled task,” or a user-defined label while consistently separating foreground conversations from heartbeat, cron, subagent, ACP, hook, harness, dreaming, and other background sessions.

## Evidence

- Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxejb7fq2y7360aqstaebmvk`: 26 focused tests passed across the Gateway projection, real `sessions.list` RPC path, plugin-runtime guard, and protocol schema.
- `oxfmt --check` passed for all 12 touched TypeScript files.

- Focused `check:changed` passed conflict, LOC, attribution, dependency, formatting, SDK-baseline, package-patch, and production typecheck gates; the core-test typecheck also reported two unrelated `auth-choice.plugin-providers.test.ts` baseline errors.

target.title: refactor(config): add canonical group-policy scope-tree resolver and migrate the first six channels
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

16 channel plugins each answer the same group-policy questions — effective `requireMention`, tool policy (including sender-scoped tools), intro hints — through a mix of one shared resolver and private per-channel walkers over channel-specific config nests. Same decision, many implementations, measurable drift.

## Why This Change Was Made

This PR carries stage 1 plus the first two channel batches of the approved group-policy scope normalization (originally staged as #106819 → #106830 → this; consolidated to one landing because each stacked landing pays a full CI + generated-baseline cycle against a fast-moving main — the inner PRs will be closed as landed-via with this commit):

1. **Core ScopeTree resolver** (`src/config/group-scope-tree.ts`): flat keyed scope nodes + channel-ordered paths (a nested tree cannot express telegram's wildcard-group-topic-outranks-exact-scalar precedence), most-specific-wins scalars with before-/after-config override ordering identical to the existing shared resolver, per-level `toolsBySender` → `tools` whole-object cascade reusing `resolveToolsBySender` verbatim, plus `buildChannelGroupsScopeTree` (13+ channels share the flat `groups` shape) and `resolveScopeKeyCaseInsensitive` (exact beats case-insensitive; wildcard lives in the defaults node). Exported via `openclaw/plugin-sdk/channel-policy`; surface budgets bumped by the exact delta with citation comments.
2. **Batch 1 — googlechat, imessage, whatsapp** (pure delegates): adapters now build a tree and emit a single-scope path; account scoping stays core-owned via `resolveChannelGroups`, preserving the single-account empty-`groups:{}` fallback quirk. Each plugin module ended smaller than before.
3. **Batch 2 — line, qqbot, mattermost** (one twist each): LINE's prefixed-key candidate pre-resolution feeds the scope path; QQBot's case-insensitive group match resolves at path-build time; Mattermost forwards its chatmode-derived requireMention override as a resolver parameter with after-config ordering (groups config beats chatmode; chatmode beats the final default).

## User Impact

None — strict behavior parity, pinned by table-driven tests per channel (exact/wildcard/absent, account override, single-account fallback, sender-scoped tools with `messageProvider` gating, LINE candidate precedence, QQBot exact-beats-CI and wildcard-never-CI-matched, Mattermost chatmode-vs-groups precedence). Group ids are matched untrimmed, exactly as before. Six of sixteen channels are now on the canonical resolver; remaining batches (zalo/irc/nextcloud-talk, zalouser/slack/matrix, feishu/msteams, discord, telegram) follow, after which ~600 LOC of per-channel walkers and the duplicate discord fallback in core get deleted.

## Evidence

- Blacksmith Testbox per stage: `group-scope-tree`/`group-policy`/`plugin-sdk` suites, then `extensions/googlechat extensions/imessage extensions/whatsapp`, then `extensions/line extensions/qqbot extensions/mattermost` (1,572 tests in the batch-2 run) — all green; `check:changed` lanes green each round; `plugin-sdk-surface-report --check` verified exact on the final rebased tree with the regenerated API baseline hash committed.
- Autoreview (codex gpt-5.6-sol, xhigh, per stage): three clean passes — "patch is correct" 0.88 (core), 0.86 (batch 1), 0.86 (batch 2); zero actionable findings across all three.
- Hosted CI green on the pre-rebase heads (one unrelated agents-core flake and one media download-timeout flake rerun to green); fresh CI running on the rebased head.

target.title: feat(config): add canonical group-policy scope-tree resolver
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

16 channel plugins register a `groups` adapter answering the same questions — effective `requireMention`, tool policy (including sender-scoped tools), group intro hints — but only 9 delegate to the shared resolver in `src/config/group-policy.ts`. The rest ship private walkers over channel-specific config nests (discord guild→channel, telegram group→topic, msteams team→channel with cross-team scan, slack/matrix/zalouser candidate matching): same decision, many implementations, measurable drift (e.g. adapter paths that can never match `channel:`-prefixed `toolsBySender` keys while the core fallback can).

## Why This Change Was Made

Stage 1 of the group-policy scope normalization design (load-time canonical model, zero user-visible config change): a `ScopeTree` of flat keyed scope nodes plus channel-ordered scope paths, with core-owned resolvers for requireMention (most-specific-wins, override-order semantics identical to `resolveChannelGroupRequireMention`), tool policy (per-level `toolsBySender` → `tools`, whole-object override, reusing `resolveToolsBySender` verbatim as the sender engine), and intro hints. Flat keys instead of a nested tree are deliberate: telegram's real precedence lets a wildcard-group topic node outrank an exact-group scalar, which a nested walk cannot express; channels encode precedence in the path they emit. Runtime overrides stay resolver parameters, never tree data. Follow-up PRs migrate channels in parity-tested batches and delete the per-channel walkers (~600 LOC across 11 files).

## User Impact

None yet — no callers are wired in this PR; behavior is unchanged. The new resolvers are exported via `openclaw/plugin-sdk/channel-policy` (surface budgets bumped by the exact delta with a citation comment) so channel migrations can adopt them.

target.title: fix(sessions): keep dirty transcript search from blocking the gateway
target.body:
Closes #105735

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where searching a session with a dirty transcript index could block the Gateway event loop while the index was rebuilt.

The rebuild began synchronously inside `searchSessionTranscripts`. Its initial SQLite work, transcript parsing, and index writes ran before the async function reached its first yield. Deferring that same work with `setImmediate` would only move the stall to the next event-loop turn.

## Why This Change Was Made

Dirty-index reconciliation now runs in a packaged worker, while transcript search returns promptly with `indexing: true`.

The worker plans outside transactions and applies short, bounded write batches protected by a database-owned claim generation. Transcript mutations invalidate an active claim, and reconciliation performs a final authoritative revision check before clearing the dirty state.

A process-wide single-slot queue bounds worker concurrency. Planning and write progress have separate watchdogs; failure or timeout releases the slot for a later retry. There is no large synchronous fallback when worker startup fails.

Normal clean-index searches and synchronous indexing of ordinary transcript appends are unchanged.

## User Impact

Gateway requests and timers remain responsive while a dirty transcript index is rebuilt. Once reconciliation finishes, transcript search returns the correctly rebuilt index.

Concurrent appends, rewinds, replacements, deletions, and reconciliation attempts cannot incorrectly mark stale index contents clean.

## Evidence

Focused regression and packaging tests:

```text
OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  src/config/sessions/session-transcript-search.test.ts \
  src/infra/tsdown-config.test.ts \
  --reporter=verbose \
  --maxWorkers=1
```

Result: 38 tests passed.

The regression coverage proves:

- Event-loop heartbeats continue after reconciliation is actively underway.
- Search eventually returns the rebuilt transcript index.
- Two database connections cannot concurrently own the same rebuild.
- Append, rewind, same-count replacement, and deletion races invalidate stale work.
- Large unrelated FTS contents do not cause long write-lock scans.
- Abandoned claims and nonresponding workers recover through bounded timeouts.
- Source, stable distribution, and hashed distribution worker paths resolve correctly.

Additional validation:

- `pnpm build` passed and emitted the transcript reconciliation worker.
- `pnpm check` passed.
- Fresh branch-mode autoreview against `origin/main` completed with no actionable findings.

## Suggested Review Order

1. `src/config/sessions/session-transcript-reconcile.ts` — claim lifecycle, planning, bounded writes, and final authoritative check.
2. `src/config/sessions/session-transcript-search.ts` — worker queue, deduplication, watchdogs, and search behavior.
3. `src/config/sessions/session-transcript-index.ts` — transcript mutations invalidating active claims.
4. `src/config/sessions/session-transcript-search.test.ts` — responsiveness, concurrency, race, and recovery proof.
5. `src/config/sessions/session-transcript-reconcile.worker.ts` — worker entry and message settlement.
6. `tsdown.config.ts`, `scripts/release-check.ts`, and `src/infra/tsdown-config.test.ts` — packaging and release inventory.

## AI Assistance

This change was developed with Codex assistance. The implementation was reviewed against repository guidance, validated with focused regression tests plus build/check gates, and passed a fresh branch-mode autoreview.

## Real behavior proof

Exact head `af68cb535507a379b18fe12c4c72c8b95b5f7f2f` was exercised through a real packaged Gateway process and its WebSocket RPC boundary using a temporary state directory. The setup used 100,000 synthetic transcript message events, then removed only the derived FTS and index-state rows to reproduce a dirty upgrade/rebuild state. No model or provider call was involved.

Redacted client transcript:

```text
{"event":"initial_search","gatewayRpcMs":687,"indexing":true,"resultCount":0}
{"event":"gateway_turn","turn":1,"healthRpcMs":194,"healthResponded":true,"searchRpcMs":351,"indexing":true,"resultCount":0}
{"event":"gateway_turn","turn":2,"healthRpcMs":5,"healthResponded":true,"searchRpcMs":311,"indexing":true,"resultCount":0}
{"event":"gateway_turn","turn":3,"healthRpcMs":3,"healthResponded":true,"searchRpcMs":275,"indexing":true,"resultCount":0}
{"event":"gateway_turn","turn":4,"healthRpcMs":4,"healthResponded":true,"searchRpcMs":251,"indexing":true,"resultCount":0}
{"event":"gateway_turn","turn":5,"healthRpcMs":3,"healthResponded":true,"searchRpcMs":272,"indexing":true,"resultCount":0}
{"event":"initial_search","gatewayRpcMs":885,"indexing":false,"resultCount":1}
{"event":"gateway_turn","turn":1,"healthRpcMs":11,"healthResponded":true,"searchRpcMs":1068,"indexing":false,"resultCount":1}
```

The Gateway then shut down cleanly and the synthetic state was removed.

target.title: fix(secrets): collect persona-level TTS provider SecretRefs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Persona-level TTS provider API keys were not collected as SecretRefs and agent persona registry paths bound the wrong path segment as providerId (literal `providers` instead of `elevenlabs`). That breaks secrets plan/audit and runtime resolution for agent persona TTS keys.

Fixes #89607

## Summary

The secret collector walks `messages.tts.providers.*.apiKey` but does not walk `messages.tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey` or `agents.list[].tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey`. When a persona overrides the TTS provider config with a file-source SecretRef, the secret resolver never sees the ref, so the `apiKey` reaches the plugin as an unresolved object instead of the actual key string. The plugin then reports `not configured`.

This fix:
- Adds persona-level provider iteration in `collectTtsApiKeyAssignments`
- Registers two new target paths in the secret target registry (`messages.tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey` and `agents.list[].tts.personas.*.providers.*.apiKey`)
- Extends `hasAgentRuntimeSecretRefs` to detect persona-level TTS refs
- Adds 5 regression tests covering top-level, persona-level, combined, empty-persona, and agent-level persona paths

Closes #89607

## Evidence

target.title: fix(tools-manager): use BigInt for lossless Content-Length comparison
target.body:
## Summary
Replace `Number()` + `isSafeInteger` with `BigInt()` for lossless Content-Length comparison in `downloadFile`.

## What Problem This Solves
`Number()` can lose precision when parsing large integer strings (≥16 digits). The existing `CONTENT_LENGTH_RE` regex `/^\d+$/` matches arbitrarily long digit strings with no upper bound, but `Number("9007199254740993")` returns `9007199254740992` — a different value.

Although `isSafeInteger` catches most precision-loss cases (any value that rounds above `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`), relying on `Number()` for integer comparison is fragile. A Content-Length string of 20+ digits like `"99999999999999999999"` becomes `100000000000000000000` through `Number()` — completely wrong.

In practice `MAX_ARCHIVE_BYTES` is 100 MB (~10⁸), so any oversized Content-Length is caught by the numeric comparison long before precision becomes an issue. This is a **correctness hardening** — using the right tool (`BigInt`) for integer comparison so the code is obviously correct at all scales.

**Code evidence**: in `src/agents/utils/tools-manager.ts:187-188`, the current code parses Content-Length through `Number()` which is not guaranteed lossless for arbitrary-length digit strings.

## Root Cause
The code was written using `Number()` for integer parsing, which is lossy for values beyond 2⁵³ − 1 (`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` = 9,007,199,254,740,991). The `isSafeInteger` guard partially mitigates this but:
1. It rejects values for the wrong reason (precision loss vs size cap)
2. The error message says "exceeds byte limit" when actually the value can't be accurately parsed
3. It relies on an indirect property (safe integer vs range check) rather than comparing the value directly

## Why This Fix
**Chosen approach**: `BigInt(contentLength) > BigInt(maxBytes)` — one-line replacement.

- **Correct**: `BigInt` preserves the exact integer from any digit string
- **Simpler**: replaces two conditions (`!isSafeInteger || > maxBytes`) with one (`> maxBytes`)
- **Proven**: `BigInt` is already used elsewhere in the codebase (`src/infra/kysely-sync.ts` etc.)
- **Minimal**: 2 lines removed, 1 line added

Alternatives considered:
- String length pre-check: avoids the problem but is ad-hoc
- `BigInt` + fallback: unnecessary — `BigInt` is well-supported in Node 22

## User Impact
No user-visible change. The existing behavior was already correct for all practical Content-Length values (≤ a few GB). This fix hardens the code against theoretically large Content-Length headers and makes the intent clearer.

## Evidence
- **Before (Number() approach)**: `Number("9007199254740993")` → `9007199254740992` (precision LOST). `Number("99999999999999999999")` → `100000000000000000000` (massively wrong). ❌ FAIL
- **After (BigInt() approach)**: `BigInt("9007199254740993")` → `9007199254740993n` (exact). `BigInt("99999999999999999999")` → `99999999999999999999n` (exact). ✓ PASS

## Real Behavior Proof

### Before (Number() approach — precision loss)
```bash
$ node --import tsx proof.mjs
============================================================
Content-Length precision loss demonstration
============================================================
Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER = 9007199254740991

--- Case 1: Large Content-Length (above MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) ---
Content-Length header: "9007199254740993"
Number("9007199254740993") = 9007199254740992
Actual BigInt value : 9007199254740993
Precision preserved?  : NO — LOST!

Old code (Number + isSafeInteger):
  declaredBytes = Number("9007199254740993") = 9007199254740992
  isSafeInteger(9007199254740992) = false
  => REJECT (declaredBytes=9007199254740992, reason="exceeds cap or not safe integer")

--- Case 3: 20-digit Content-Length ---
Number("99999999999999999999") = 100000000000000000000
Number result accurate?  NO — massively wrong!

FAIL: Number() lost precision on Content-Length '9007199254740993'
FAIL: Number() returned wrong value for 20-digit Content-Length
```

### After (BigInt() comparison — exact)
```bash
$ node --import tsx proof.mjs
--- Case 1: Large Content-Length (above MAX_SAFE_INTEGER) ---
New code (BigInt comparison):
  BigInt("9007199254740993") = 9007199254740993n
  9007199254740993n > 10n = true
  => REJECT (reason="exceeds cap")

--- Case 2: Normal Content-Length (within safe range) ---
Old: ACCEPT  |  New: ACCEPT

PASS: BigInt() preserves exact value: 9007199254740993n
```

## Tests and Validation
- `pnpm check` passed
- `vitest run src/agents/utils/tools-manager.test.ts` — 18 tests passed (2 new: large Content-Length rejection)
- Added regression test: "rejects downloads with large Content-Length that would lose precision with Number()"

target.title: fix(dreaming): drop heartbeat assistant responses from dream corpus
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The dreaming ingestion pipeline filters heartbeat **user** messages (containing `[OpenClaw heartbeat poll]`) via `sanitizeSessionText`, but the paired **assistant** response was only dropped when it was the exact string `HEARTBEAT_OK`. Local models frequently respond with natural-language acknowledgments (e.g. "Heartbeat received. Main is active.") which pass through the sanitizer unchanged and enter the dream corpus as low-confidence memory snippets.

See issue #103720.

## Why This Change Was Made

The original text-based heartbeat detection was user-spoofable (anyone could type the heartbeat marker and trigger the drop). The fix uses **runtime provenance** (`provenance: { kind: "heartbeat" }`) attached at the source in `get-reply-run.ts`, which cannot be spoofed by user input.

For existing workspaces with heartbeat contamination, the `doctor` audit/repair system:
- Scans session-corpus files for heartbeat-derived lines via source refs
- Removes only heartbeat lines while preserving normal content
- Handles **both file-backed sessions** (`.jsonl` paths) and **SQLite-backed sessions** (logical paths without extension) via a fallback to `loadTranscriptEventsSync`
- Avoids clearing session ingestion checkpoints to prevent corpus duplication on re-ingestion
- Falls through to self-ingestion narrative content checks even when heartbeat contamination is found

## User Impact

- **No visible change** for users without heartbeat contamination
- **Lower memory noise** for users with heartbeat-enabled sessions — average 0.58-confidence heartbeat-derived entries are removed from dream corpus
- **One-time cleanup** via `openclaw doctor` for existing workspaces
- **No data loss** — heartbeat lines are archived before removal, normal corpus lines are preserved

## Evidence

### Forward Prevention (Provenance-based)
- Heartbeat turns carry `provenance: { kind: "heartbeat" }` attached at the source in `get-reply-run.ts`
- `buildSessionEntry` checks `message.provenance.kind === "heartbeat"` instead of text-matching user content
- When a heartbeat user message is filtered, the immediately following assistant response is also dropped via a `pendingHeartbeatUserDrop` flag
- Cross-message coupling is gated by runtime provenance (not user-spoofable text per PR #70737)

### Backward Repair (Targeted Doctor Audit)
- `auditDreamingArtifacts` + `repairDreamingArtifacts` functions available via `openclaw doctor`
- Detects and archives heartbeat-derived session-corpus entries, contaminated session-ingestion state, and duplicate diary entries
- Handles both file-backed and SQLite logical session paths in corpus references

### Validation
- [x] Format: `oxfmt --check` passes
- [x] Lint: `oxlint --deny curly` passes
- [x] Extension tests: 63 files, 1046/1046 tests pass
- [x] Type check: `tsgo` passes
- [x] LOC ratchet: both files under 500 lines
- [x] Autoreview: 2 P1s fixed (checkpoint clearing, path resolution), 2 remaining known issues in pre-existing code

## Files Changed

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/session-files.ts` | `pendingHeartbeatUserDrop` flag + provenance-based heartbeat detection |
| `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/session-files.test.ts` | Tests: heartbeat provenance filtering |
| `src/sessions/input-provenance.ts` | Export heartbeat provenance kind constant |
| `src/auto-reply/reply/get-reply-run.ts` | Attach `provenance: { kind: "heartbeat" }` to heartbeat replies |
| `extensions/memory-core/src/dreaming-repair.ts` | Audit + repair functions for dreaming artifacts |
| `extensions/memory-core/src/dreaming-repair-utils.ts` | New: helper utilities extracted for LOC ratchet |
| `extensions/memory-core/src/dreaming-repair.test.ts` | Tests for dreaming repair |
| `src/commands/doctor-memory-search.ts` | Integrate dreaming audit/repair into doctor command |
| `src/commands/doctor-memory-search.test.ts` | Update mocks for new imports |

target.title: fix(qa-channel): add timeout to qa-bus state guarded fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `getQaBusState` called `fetchWithSsrFGuard` with no `timeoutMs` and no `AbortSignal`, so a loopback qa-bus peer that accepted TCP but never returned headers could hang Gateway/QA tooling forever (body idle caps never start).

## Why This Change Was Made

- Pass `timeoutMs: QA_BUS_STATE_TIMEOUT_MS` (10s) through the existing guarded fetch, matching Feishu registration / similar Type C hang floors.
- Optional `options.timeoutMs` overrides for hermetic hang regressions only; production callers omit it.
- No new config/env surface.

## User Impact

**Before:** A hung qa-bus `/v1/state` peer could pin state inspection indefinitely.

**After:** State fetches fail closed after 10s with `TimeoutError` so QA/monitor loops can continue.

## Evidence

Head: `cadb067c5abd997f396198b41094afd7e150eff2`

### Executable negative control + fix proof

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qa-channel/src/bus-client.test.ts -- --run -t "negative control|never returns headers" --reporter=verbose
```

```text
[qa-channel bus-state negative control] outcome=still-pending wait_ms=200 without_timeoutMs=true
[qa-channel bus-state hang proof] timed_out=true name=TimeoutError elapsed_ms=85 production_timeout_ms=10000
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed | 6 skipped (8)
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** `/v1/state` guarded fetch hangs forever when peer accepts TCP but never returns headers.
- **Canonical path:** `getQaBusState` → production `fetchWithSsrFGuard` with `timeoutMs: QA_BUS_STATE_TIMEOUT_MS` (10s) / test override.
- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime HTTP; real loopback `node:http` never-headers peer; production SSRF-guarded transport (negative control calls `fetchWithSsrFGuard` with **no** `timeoutMs`).
- **After fix:** `TimeoutError` in ~80ms with override; production floor is the exported 10s constant.

target.title: fix(polls): add default maximum poll option count
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: Matrix polls had no outbound `pollMaxOptions` limit while the Matrix protocol (MSC3381) caps poll options at 20. Other channels (Discord=10, WhatsApp=12, MS Teams=12, Telegram=12) all declare their protocol limits.
- Solution: Declare `pollMaxOptions: 20` in Matrix-owned outbound code and pass `maxOptions: 20` explicitly in `buildPollStartContent`. The shared `normalizePollInput` helper's public contract is unchanged: omitting `maxOptions` means no limit, preserving caller-controlled behavior.
- What changed:
  - `extensions/matrix/src/channel.ts` — added `pollMaxOptions: 20` to `matrixChannelOutbound`
  - `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/poll-types.ts` — `buildPollStartContent` passes `maxOptions: 20` explicitly to `normalizePollInput`
  - `src/polls.test.ts` — locks in omitted-`maxOptions` = no limit contract
  - `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/poll-types.test.ts` — 20-option boundary tests (accept 20, reject 21)
  - `extensions/matrix/src/channel.message-adapter.test.ts` — asserts `pollMaxOptions` on static outbound adapter
- What did NOT change: `normalizePollInput` omitted-limit semantics; `src/polls.ts`; other channel implementations; no unrelated UI/avatar changes.

## ClawSweeper review fixes (all P1 findings addressed)

- **P1: Keep the generic poll limit caller-configured** — `src/polls.ts` is untouched. `normalizePollInput` retains its original contract: omitting `maxOptions` means no limit. The 20-option Matrix protocol limit lives entirely in Matrix-owned code: `matrixChannelOutbound.pollMaxOptions = 20` and `buildPollStartContent(..., { maxOptions: 20 })`. A regression test locks in the omitted-limit = no limit behavior.
- **P1: Drop the unrelated avatar commit** — The branch has been force-pushed from a clean `origin/main` base. All unrelated Control UI avatar changes from #104912 are removed.
- **P1: Rebase to clean mergeable head** — The branch is now a single commit on top of latest `origin/main`, no conflicts.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Matrix polls were missing the 20-option protocol limit. Now enforced at the Matrix boundary.
- **Real environment tested:** Vitest unit tests for Matrix poll types, Matrix outbound adapter, and shared poll helper contract.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
  ```bash
  pnpm test src/polls.test.ts
  pnpm test extensions/matrix/src/matrix/poll-types.test.ts
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/matrix/src/channel.message-adapter.test.ts
  ```

- **Evidence after fix:**
  ```text
  # src/polls.test.ts — 7 passed

  - "declares a 20-option poll maximum..." → outbound.pollMaxOptions = 20 ✓
  ```

## Regression Test Plan

target.title: fix(reef): bound relay HTTP JSON response body reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Reef users could have the relay HTTP client buffer an unbounded JSON response body when a misbehaving or hostile relay returned oversized success or error payloads on `ReefTransportClient` request paths (auth, friends, mail pull/send/ack).

Related sibling surface: open #106439 bounds Reef *guard* provider responses in `extensions/reef/protocol/guard-adapters.ts`; this PR covers the separate relay transport client in `extensions/reef/src/transport.ts`, which still used unbounded `response.json()`.

## Why This Change Was Made

`ReefTransportClient.request` now reads JSON through the shared `readProviderJsonResponse` helper from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/provider-http`:

- success bodies capped at 16 MiB (`reef.relay`)
- error bodies capped at 64 KiB (`reef.relay.error`), with the existing status-code fallback preserved when the error body is missing, malformed, or oversized

Oversized streams are cancelled before the remainder is buffered. Non-goal: changing guard adapters (owned by #106439) or adding new config.

## User Impact

Reef relay HTTP calls fail closed on oversized JSON instead of allocating unbounded memory. Normal-sized relay responses and bounded error messages continue to work as before.

## Evidence

Head: `7d4ab0a3461a71021bd0d0ba53d5aade8573206f`

**Head:** `f8d35557ae69c3e457b601cbe2bc535049689032`

**Behavior addressed:** Hostile/oversized relay JSON no longer forces unbounded `response.json()` allocation; streams cancel after the byte budget.

**Real environment tested:** Linux WSL2, Node `v22.22.0`, local checkout of this branch.

### Path-level proof (production `ReefTransportClient` + negative control)

```text
$ ./node_modules/.bin/tsx proof-reef-relay-json-bound.ts

error overflow name=ReefRelayError status=503 message=relay HTTP 503 cancelled=true emittedBytes=81920
negative control response.json() cancelled=false emittedBytes=262144
ok
```

Interpretation:

- success path offered ~20 MiB, cancelled after `16908288` bytes (~16 MiB + one 64 KiB chunk)
- error path offered 128 KiB against a 64 KiB cap, cancelled after `81920` bytes, still threw `ReefRelayError` with `relay HTTP 503`
- negative control: the same tracked-stream shape drained fully under unbounded `response.json()` with `cancelled=false`

target.title: fix(whatsapp): add chunk-idle timeout to inbound media download
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where WhatsApp inbound media downloads that stall after Baileys returns a stream (headers/start ok, then no further chunks) would block `downloadInboundMedia` forever via `saveMediaStream`'s unbounded `for await`, so inbound dispatch never produces an agent reply for that message.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Wrap the Baileys AsyncIterable with a local per-chunk idle race (production default `30_000` ms), matching Telegram's download idle floor and the LINE channel pattern (open `#86873`, different owner).
- On timeout, reject with `WhatsAppInboundMediaTimeoutError`, call `iterator.return()` so Node Readable streams are destroyed, and silence the losing `next()` to avoid `unhandledRejection`.
- Tests may pass a short `chunkTimeoutMs`; production omits it and uses the 30s floor (proven with fake timers).
- Does **not** change core `saveMediaStream` / `src/media/store.ts` (avoids competing with LINE `#86873`).
- Timeout error class stays module-private (knip unused-export gate).

No new config/env surface.

## User Impact

**Before:** A stalled WhatsApp media body could hang inbound handling for that message indefinitely.

**After:** Idle streams fail closed after 30s with a clear timeout error so the monitor loop can continue.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(codex): bound app-server websocket handshake waits at 30s
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators using Codex app-server over `websocket`/`unix` transport would hang forever on `initialize`/RPC when a peer accepted TCP but never completed the WebSocket upgrade. Pending frames never flush and the client never sees a transport exit, so the run cannot fail closed or reconnect.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Add a private `buildCodexAppServerWebSocketOptions` that sets `handshakeTimeout: 30_000` (same floor as Slack relay / Mattermost / Discord gateway).
- Both TCP and Unix upgrade paths consume that builder.
- Guard `EventEmitter` error re-emit with `listenerCount` so callers that only wait on `exit` (handshake hang paths) are not disrupted by Node's unhandled-`error` throw.
- Regressions observe production wiring in source (knip-safe) and prove stalled-handshake exit + `initialize` failure with a short test-only hang floor.

No new config/env surface.

## User Impact

**Before:** A Codex app-server endpoint that accepted TCP without completing the websocket handshake could pin `initialize`/RPC forever on that attempt.

**After:** Handshake waits fail closed after 30s (`Opening handshake has timed out` → transport `exit` / client error), so the run can stop or recover instead of hanging.

## Evidence

Head: `a02be68e1107857c4808cc9e93e1af5b10c7f1f1`

### Wiring + hang regression

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```text

[codex handshake proof] timed_out=true elapsed_ms=200 code=1006 handshakeTimeout_ms=200 production_ms=30000
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** TCP-accept / never-upgrade pins Codex app-server `initialize`/RPC with no transport exit.
- **Canonical path:** production `createWebSocketTransport` → private builder with `handshakeTimeout: CODEX_APP_SERVER_WS_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS` (30s).
- **Boundary crossed:** local-runtime TCP; real `ws` against loopback `net.Server` that accepts but never upgrades (no handshake mock).
- **Negative control:** plain `ws.WebSocket` **without** `handshakeTimeout` stays `CONNECTING` / `still-pending` after 300ms on the same fixture.
- **After fix:** short test floor exits ~200ms with code 1006; production wiring asserts the 30s constant.

target.title: fix: Control UI avatar initial breaks on emoji display names
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent's display name begins with an emoji or other astral Unicode character, the Control UI sidebar and agent selector rendered a broken or garbled avatar initial (a lone UTF-16 surrogate half / replacement character) instead of the intended glyph. This PR fixes that by using `Intl.Segmenter` to properly extract grapheme clusters.

## Summary

- **Problem**: Avatar initial used `.slice(0, 1)` (first UTF-16 code unit), breaking on emoji/astral Unicode.
- **Solution**: New `deriveAvatarInitial` helper using `Intl.Segmenter` with `granularity: "grapheme"` for complete grapheme clusters. Falls back to surrogate pair-aware extraction for browsers without `Intl.Segmenter` (Firefox 114-124).
- **What changed**: 
  - `ui/src/lib/avatar.ts` — `deriveAvatarInitial` with feature detection and fallback
  - `ui/src/components/app-sidebar.ts` — uses helper
  - `ui/src/components/agent-select.ts` — uses helper in fallback
- **What did NOT change**: ASCII names; other `.slice()` sites (ASCII-only inputs).

## Browser Compatibility

- **With Intl.Segmenter** (Firefox 125+, Chrome 87+, Safari 14.1+): Complete grapheme clusters preserved
- **Without Intl.Segmenter** (Firefox 114-124): First complete code point extracted (surrogate pair-aware)

## Evidence

**Environment**: jsdom with real Lit component rendering + Playwright E2E tests

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash

node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run ui/src/lib/avatar.test.ts ui/src/components/agent-select.test.ts

# Playwright E2E tests

```

target.title: fix(zalo): bound proxy fetcher cache to 64 entries
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Zalo `resolveZaloProxyFetch` retained one `makeProxyFetch` entry per distinct proxy URL in a process-lifetime `Map` with no eviction. Config churn or high-cardinality proxy URLs could therefore grow gateway memory without a hard bound.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Cap `proxyCache` at 64 entries using the shared `pruneMapToMaxSize` helper after every successful insert (same pattern as Nextcloud Talk room cache / MS Teams team-group cache / Mattermost opaque-target cache).
- Insertion-order eviction keeps newest proxy fetchers; cache-hit identity and empty-URL behavior are unchanged.
- Adds a focused regression that fills `max+1` distinct URLs, proves the oldest entry is rebuilt on next use, and confirms a mid-window entry still hits.

No new config/env surface. Does not change Bot API timeouts (`#104017`) or other Zalo send paths.

## User Impact

**Before:** Long-running Zalo gateways could retain an unbounded number of proxy fetcher closures as distinct proxy URLs appeared.

**After:** At most 64 distinct proxy fetchers are retained; older ones are dropped and rebuilt on next use.

## Evidence

## Summary
- Problem: Four locations decode base64 payloads before checking size limits, risking transient OOM if a provider/tool returns an oversized payload.
- Solution: Add estimate-before-decode guards where safe, preserve existing behavior contracts where compatibility matters.
- What changed:
  - `src/agents/cli-runner/helpers.ts`: writeCliImages adds maxBytes param, estimates decoded size before Buffer.from
  - `src/image-generation/image-assets.ts`: Estimates decoded size before canonicalization to avoid transient string allocation; propagates maxBytes through `generatedImageAssetFromBase64`, `generatedImageAssetFromOpenAiCompatibleEntry`, and `parseOpenAiCompatibleImageResponse`
  - `src/image-generation/openai-compatible-image-provider.ts`: Wires `resolveGeneratedMediaMaxBytes(req.cfg, "image")` into `parseOpenAiCompatibleImageResponse`
  - `extensions/openai/image-generation-provider.ts`: Wires `resolveGeneratedImageMaxBytes` into OpenAI image generation path
  - `extensions/google/image-generation-provider.ts`: Wires `resolveGeneratedImageMaxBytes` into Google image generation path
  - `extensions/openrouter/image-generation-provider.ts`: Wires `resolveGeneratedImageMaxBytes` into OpenRouter image extraction path
- What did NOT change: `resizeImage` still attempts resize before rejecting (maxBytes is an output target, not an input ceiling); `generatedMusicAssetFromBase64` still returns guaranteed result for SDK compatibility.

- **Observed result after fix:**
  1. Provider path: valid configured-size payload (100 bytes) accepted and parsed into image asset; oversized payload (6292480 bytes > 6291456 budget) rejected before decode with 0 images returned
  2. CLI image-write path: valid image (50 bytes) written to disk successfully; oversized image (6292480 bytes > 6291456 budget) rejected with error before Buffer.from allocation
  3. Provider limit propagation confirmed: `resolveGeneratedMediaMaxBytes` returns 6291456 (6 MB default), wired through `parseOpenAiCompatibleImageResponse` and all four provider paths
- **What was not tested:** Live provider API response (requires credentials); Rastermill resize (requires image processor backend). The proof exercises the actual final-head code paths with simulated provider payloads that match the real response structure.

## CI failures fixed
- **check-additional-runtime-topology-architecture**: Pre-existing Kysely guardrail violations in `src/snapshot/local-repository.ts` (not in PR diff) — fixed by rebasing on latest `upstream/main`.
- **check-docs**: `docs/docs_map.md` was out of date (not in PR diff) — fixed by rebasing on latest `upstream/main`.
- Both failures were unrelated to this PR's changes and are resolved on the rebased head. Verified locally: `pnpm lint:kysely` → "Kysely guardrails OK"; `pnpm docs:map:check` → "docs:map: docs/docs_map.md is up to date."

## Regression Test Plan
- Coverage level: Unit test
- Target test file: src/agents/cli-runner.helpers.test.ts, src/image-generation/image-assets.test.ts, src/music-generation/provider-assets.test.ts
- Scenario locked in: Oversized base64 payload rejected before canonicalization; normal payloads decode successfully; music helper returns guaranteed result.
- Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail: Tests the exact security invariant (estimate-before-decode where safe) while preserving compatibility contracts.

## Root Cause
- Root cause: Functions skipped the "estimate decoded bytes before decode" guard in some paths, and applied it incorrectly in others (blocking resize, breaking SDK contracts).
- Missing detection / guardrail: Pre-canonicalization size check in image-assets; understanding that maxBytes is an output target not an input ceiling for resizeImage; SDK compatibility requirement for music helper; provider limit propagation through all four provider paths.

target.title: perf: avoid event-loop stall during embedded_run bootstrap-context
target.body:
## Summary

Fix event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context that block the event loop for 14-22 seconds, causing message loss.

### Root causes addressed

1. **Synchronous file I/O** — `readFileSync`/`closeSync` in workspace file loading blocks the event loop while reading root bootstrap files (AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, etc.)
2. **Unbounded blocking glob walks** — `fs.glob` for extra bootstrap files traverses the entire workspace tree synchronously inside Node, including `.git`/`node_modules` directories, without yielding to the event loop
3. **Uninterrupted hook chains** — `triggerInternalHook` executes all handlers back-to-back without yielding

### Changes

**`src/agents/workspace.ts`**
- Replace sync `readFileSync`/`closeSync` with callback-based async `readFdToString`/`closeFdAsync`
- Parallelize root bootstrap file reads via `Promise.all` (previously serial `for` loop)
- Replace `fs.glob` with an async traversal walker that yields via `setImmediate` every 256 entries, so a sparse pattern like `**/AGENTS.md` over a large workspace never blocks the event loop. The walker performs no directory pruning — it walks the full tree and returns every file matching the configured patterns, with no traversal cutoff and no artificial match cap; the downstream bootstrap character budget owns content limiting.
- Preserve `fs.glob` no-match parity: a configured glob that matches nothing resolves to an empty set (not the literal pattern), so it no longer emits a phantom missing-file diagnostic; the literal `[pattern]` result is reserved for the no-glob-support fallback only.
- Preserve `fs.glob` explicit directory-symlink parity: descend a symlink only when its aligned pattern segment is literal (non-wildcard) and `realpath` confirms a directory inside the workspace root, so an explicit configured pattern like `linked/**/AGENTS.md` still reaches descendants when `linked` is an in-workspace directory symlink. Symlinks reached through a wildcard segment stay terminal (matching `fs.glob`), workspace containment rejects symlink targets that escape the root, and a `realpath` ancestor-chain guard refuses re-entry into a directory already on the descent path so an ancestor-pointing symlink (`a/loop -> a`) cannot loop.
- Suppress `closeFdAsync` rejections to avoid masking read errors on NFS/FUSE

**`src/hooks/internal-hooks.ts`** / **`src/hooks/internal-hook-dispatch.ts`**
- Keep the public `triggerInternalHook(event)` signature (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/hook-runtime`) unchanged and matching `main` — no new public parameter or exported options type.
- Move the bootstrap-only handler scheduling (`yieldBetweenHandlers` with `setImmediate` yield between handlers) and per-handler timing/slow-handler (>500ms) warning into an internal `internal-hook-dispatch` module that is not on the plugin SDK surface.

**`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts`**
- Instrument bootstrap-context substages (`workspace-file-load`, `hook-overrides`) with `performance.now` timing
- Log substage durations when total bootstrap-context exceeds 2 seconds
- Enable yielding between handlers for `agent:bootstrap` hook triggers (via the internal dispatch entrypoint)

**`src/agents/bootstrap-files.ts`** / **`src/agents/bootstrap-hooks.ts`**
- Keep the public `resolveBootstrapFilesForRun` params (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/agent-harness-runtime`) callback-free and matching `main`; route embedded-runner substage timing through an internal `resolveBootstrapFilesForRunWithTiming` variant kept off the SDK surface.
- Support the new async workspace file loading interface.

### Tests

- `workspace.test.ts` — 3 new tests for async fd read (happy path, cache hit, fd close on failure)
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — every matching file returned without an artificial cap (no directory pruning), and a regression test asserting a late-appearing match in a large tree is still loaded (no traversal cutoff)
- `handler.test.ts` — no truncation warning is emitted for large glob scans
- `internal-hooks.test.ts` — yield-between-handlers ordering, handler timing reporting, and slow handler warning exercised through the internal dispatch entrypoint
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — a no-match glob resolves to an empty set with no missing-file diagnostic (fs.glob parity)
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — explicit directory-symlink glob parity across three states (real `fs.symlink`): a literal-named directory symlink is descended and its descendants match; a `**`-reached symlink stays terminal; an ancestor-pointing (cyclic) literal symlink terminates without looping

The public plugin SDK surface is unchanged: `node scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mjs` exits 0 with no new package-exported entrypoints. All existing tests pass without modification.

### Performance impact

- Root bootstrap file loading: serial sync → parallel async (estimated 3-5x speedup for 8 files)
- Glob walks: synchronous/blocking → async with periodic `setImmediate` yields (prevents multi-second event-loop stalls on large workspaces). The walk completes fully; all configured matches are kept, and the existing bootstrap character-budget truncation handles content limiting.
- Hook chains: uninterrupted → yielded (prevents monopolizing the event loop during bootstrap)

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context loading caused by synchronous I/O and a blocking `fs.glob` walk over large workspaces, which blocks the loop and drops messages. This change makes the glob walk async/yielding so the loop stays responsive, while preserving every configured `bootstrap-extra-files` glob match (the earlier iteration of this branch added a hard 20,000-entry traversal cutoff that silently dropped late matches — that cutoff is removed here).
- **Real environment tested**: Local patched OpenClaw checkout on macOS arm64, Node.js `v24.10.0`, run via `tsx` against the real exported `loadExtraBootstrapFiles` from `src/agents/workspace.ts`. Before/after captured from two git commits on the PR branch: before = `5849e709f4` (walker with the 20,000-entry cutoff), after = `5ce395d645` (cutoff removed).
- **Real environment scenario**: A workspace of ~26,100 filesystem entries (a 3-tier tree, 30×30×28 filler files) with a single configured-glob target `AGENTS.md` planted in the subtree the depth-first walker drains last, so the target is only reached after more than 20,000 visited entries. A 5ms repeating timer runs during the load as an event-loop liveness probe (steady ticks ⇒ the loop never stalled).
- **Failing proof before fix**: commit `5849e709f4` (cutoff present):
  ```
  approx filesystem entries: ~26100 (old cutoff was 20000)
  elapsed: 82.9ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 16 (loop responsive)
  matched bootstrap files returned: 0
  deep AGENTS.md (past old 20k cutoff) loaded: false
  RESULT: late configured glob match was DROPPED (pre-fix behavior)
  ```
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
  ```
  # against the patched checkout (commit 5ce395d645) a script that builds the
  # ~26,100-entry workspace, starts a 5ms liveness timer, then calls the real
  # loadExtraBootstrapFiles(root, ["**/AGENTS.md"]) and checks the deep match:
  npx tsx proof-live.mts
  ```
- **Evidence after fix**: terminal output from `node`/`tsx` against commit `5ce395d645` (cutoff removed):
  ```
  approx filesystem entries: ~26100 (old cutoff was 20000)
  elapsed: 99.4ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 20 (loop responsive)
  matched bootstrap files returned: 1
  deep AGENTS.md (past old 20k cutoff) loaded: true
  RESULT: configured glob match beyond old cutoff is PRESERVED; event loop stayed live
  ```
- **Observed result after fix**: With the cutoff removed, the configured `**/AGENTS.md` match located past the old 20,000-entry frontier is now loaded (1 file returned vs 0 before in the terminal output above), so existing broad `bootstrap-extra-files` configs no longer silently lose AGENTS.md/TOOLS.md context. The liveness timer kept ticking throughout the async walk (20 ticks during the ~99ms load), confirming the periodic `setImmediate` yields — not the cutoff — are what keep the event loop responsive.
- **What was not tested**: No full live `embedded_run` with active channel connections was driven end-to-end; this proof exercises the real glob-resolution code path and event-loop liveness directly rather than through a connected channel. The focused regression coverage lives in `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` and `handler.test.ts`.

### Directory-symlink glob parity proof

- **Behavior addressed**: The cooperative walker only descended `Dirent.isDirectory()` entries and emitted symlinks as leaf candidates, so an explicit configured pattern such as `linked/**/AGENTS.md` no longer reached descendants when `linked` is an in-workspace directory symlink — Node's `fs.glob` resolves that case, so the walker silently dropped configured bootstrap context. The walker now descends a literal-named path-segment symlink when `realpath` confirms a directory inside the workspace, keeps wildcard-reached symlinks terminal, and guards against ancestor cycles.
- **Real environment tested**: Local patched OpenClaw checkout on macOS arm64, Node.js `v24.10.0`. Three regression tests build real temp directories with real `fs.symlink` links and drive the real exported extra-bootstrap glob resolver.
- **Steps run**: `npx vitest run src/agents/workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts src/agents/workspace.test.ts`
- **Observed result**: `Test Files 4 passed (4)`, `Tests 156 passed (156)`. The three symlink states are covered: (a) literal-named directory symlink is descended and its descendants match; (b) a `**`-reached symlink stays terminal; (c) an ancestor-pointing (cyclic) literal symlink terminates without looping (guarded by a 15s timeout). A TDD red check confirmed test (a) fails on the pre-fix walker (missing the `linked/` descendants) and passes after the fix; `tsgo:core` exits 0 and `oxfmt --check` reports both files formatted.
- **What was not tested**: Behavior on Windows/`EPERM`/`ENOSYS` filesystems where symlink creation is unavailable — those cases skip cleanly rather than assert.

Closes #87509
